passages.text: In 1566 a twenty-year-old Danish nobleman named Tycho Brahe lost part of his nose in a sword duel, reportedly after an altercation over mathematics, and wore a metal prosthesis for the rest of his life. He is remembered for far more than that disfigurement. In 1576 the Danish king bestowed on him the island of Hven, where he built Uraniborg, an observatory furnished with colossal instruments for gauging the positions of stars and planets. Tycho worked before the advent of the telescope, yet his naked-eye measurements surpassed in precision any made before. He also spurned the Sun-centered system advanced by Copernicus, preferring a hybrid scheme in which the planets circled the Sun while the Sun orbited a stationary Earth. Ironically, after his death in 1601 his assistant Johannes Kepler used Tycho's own records to show that the planets trace ellipses around the Sun, a result that bolstered the very theory Tycho had repudiated.

The naked mole-rat, a nearly hairless rodent from the dry grasslands of East Africa, looks like something assembled from spare parts, yet biologists regard it as one of the most singular mammals alive. It lives out its existence entirely underground in colonies of dozens or even hundreds of animals, and, as in colonies of bees and ants, each colony has a single breeding female, the queen, while the others excavate tunnels, forage for roots, and defend the nest. It is also astonishingly long-lived. A mouse of comparable size seldom survives more than a few years, but naked mole-rats in captivity have lived beyond thirty, and they are strikingly resistant to cancer. In a 2017 experiment they survived eighteen minutes with no oxygen at all, apparently by switching to a metabolic pathway more characteristic of plants. Researchers hope that deciphering such capacities might one day help safeguard human tissue after heart attacks and strokes.

For more than a century, the painted caves of Europe, with their bison, horses, and lions, were hailed as the birthplace of figurative art. Discoveries on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi have progressively eroded that assumption. In 2024 researchers reported that a faded red painting in a limestone cave there, depicting three human-like figures apparently interacting with a wild pig, was at least 51,200 years old. That means it predates any known cave art in Europe by many thousands of years. The team dated the image not from the pigment itself but from thin mineral crusts that had accreted over it, using a refined laser technique that measures the slow decay of uranium in such deposits. Because the crusts grew on top of the paint, the painting must be older still — and the scene is significant for another reason. It appears to tell a story, suggesting that the human propensity for narrating events in pictures is far more ancient than once believed.

Hearing an assertion more than once makes it seem more plausible, even when it is false; psychologists first documented this illusory truth effect in 1977, when volunteers assessed the truth of trivia statements over several sessions. Statements they had seen before were deemed more likely to be true than new ones, irrespective of whether they were accurate. The explanation lies in what researchers call processing fluency. A familiar claim is easier for the mind to process, and that ease is misconstrued as a sign of truth. More disquieting, a later study found that repetition could amplify belief even in claims that contradicted facts the participants already knew. The effect has far-reaching implications for advertising and political messaging, and it complicates efforts to rectify misinformation. A correction that repeats a myth in order to refute it may inadvertently make the myth more familiar. For that reason, some experts advocate stating the accurate information first and alluding to the falsehood only briefly.

When European ships began visiting Rapa Nui, the Pacific island also called Easter Island, in the eighteenth century, visitors described its colossal stone statues but made no mention of writing. Only in the 1860s did a missionary report wooden tablets inscribed with rows of small carved signs: birds, fish, human figures, and geometric shapes. The script, known as rongorongo, survives on about two dozen objects now dispersed among museums around the world, and no one has deciphered it. By the mid-1860s slave raids and epidemics had ravaged the population, killing, it is thought, those who could read the signs. Some scholars have contended that rongorongo was invented only after the islanders watched Spanish officials sign a decree annexing the island in 1770. A 2024 study complicated that hypothesis: radiocarbon dating showed that the wood of one tablet came from a tree cut down well before European contact, although the signs themselves could have been carved later.

Jakarta, home to more than ten million people, is among the fastest-sinking large cities on Earth. Decades of pumping groundwater have caused the soft ground beneath parts of the city to subside by several centimeters a year, and in places by far more, while the sea along its coast is rising. Floods are chronic and traffic is notoriously bad. In 2019 Indonesia's president announced that the country would build an entirely new capital, later named Nusantara, on the island of Borneo. The government touted it as a green, smart city surrounded by forest, and in August 2024 Independence Day was commemorated there for the first time. The project has nevertheless faced persistent skepticism. Private investment has arrived more slowly than hoped, construction has lagged, and conservation groups worry about deforestation and the rights of local communities. Relocating government offices, critics add, will do little to alleviate the plight of the millions who remain in Jakarta.

In 1929 the Belgian painter René Magritte exhibited a meticulously painted picture of a tobacco pipe, smooth and brown against a plain background, as lifelike as an illustration in a shop catalogue. Beneath it, in neat handwriting, he added a sentence in French that translates as This is not a pipe. Viewers were perplexed and some were indignant: of course it was a pipe, they protested. Magritte's point was simple once grasped. The object on the canvas was not a pipe but a picture of one, a few ounces of pigment daubed on a flat surface; no one could fill it with tobacco. The title he gave the work, The Treachery of Images, suggests how readily we conflate the two. Decades later the philosopher Michel Foucault wrote a short book about the painting, and it remains a canonical example in discussions of how words and images refer to the world. Magritte had painted, in effect, <u>a pipe that no one will ever smoke</u>.

For decades, the story of nuclear power in many Western countries was one of retrenchment — projects ran years behind schedule, costs ballooned, and accidents such as Fukushima in 2011 hardened public opposition. Recently, however, the technology has enjoyed a resurgence of interest, driven by anxieties about climate change and energy security, and much of the enthusiasm has coalesced around small modular reactors, or SMRs. Instead of building a gigantic plant on site as a one-off engineering project, the idea is to manufacture smaller reactor units in factories and ship them for assembly, much as aircraft are fabricated on production lines. Proponents contend that standardized designs would allow costs to fall as builders gain experience, and that small units could be situated near factories or on the sites of decommissioned coal plants. The economics, however, remain unproven and the obstacles substantial. In 2023 one of the most advanced American projects, backed by a group of utilities in Utah, was cancelled after its projected price of electricity soared and too few buyers signed up. Critics note that the savings anticipated from factory production hinge on building many units of the same design, yet no one wants to place the first orders until those savings have been demonstrated. Until that ____ is broken, small reactors may look more attractive on paper than on the grid.

When Franz Kafka died of tuberculosis in 1924, he left his closest friend, the writer Max Brod, an unequivocal instruction: everything he had not published, including diaries, letters, and manuscripts, was to be burned unread. Brod refused. In subsequent years he edited and published the unfinished novels The Trial, The Castle, and Amerika, which transformed an obscure Prague insurance official into one of the most influential writers of the twentieth century. Was Brod's disobedience a betrayal or an act of loyalty? Brod himself offered a rationale. He said he had told Kafka years earlier that he would never carry out such a request, and that Kafka, knowing this, would have chosen a different executor had he truly wanted the papers destroyed. On this view, Kafka's <u>putative</u> wish to destroy his work was less a command than a gesture of self-doubt. Some critics remain ambivalent; a writer's wishes about his own work, they argue, should count for something, even if the world profits by disregarding them. The story has a curious sequel: when Brod fled the Nazis in 1939, he carried a suitcase of Kafka's papers to Palestine, and decades of litigation followed before most of them reached the National Library of Israel.

Almost all the data that crosses the oceans, from video calls to bank transfers, travels not through satellites but through fiber-optic cables lying on the seabed. Several hundred such cables connect the continents, and in deep water many are no thicker than a garden hose — and surprisingly vulnerable. Every year a considerable number are damaged, mostly by accident, when fishing trawlers drag their nets or ships drop anchor in the wrong place. Repair ships can usually restore service within days or weeks, and because traffic is rerouted through other lines, ordinary users rarely notice. Recent incidents have nevertheless turned cables into a strategic concern. In late 2024 several cables and a power line under the Baltic Sea were damaged within a few weeks, each time near the route of a merchant ship that had apparently dragged its anchor along the seabed. Finnish authorities boarded one tanker suspected of causing the damage. Proof of deliberate sabotage, however, is notoriously elusive: an anchor dragged by a negligent crew leaves much the same trace as one dragged on purpose. Governments have responded by intensifying naval patrols, mapping vulnerable routes, and encouraging companies to lay redundant lines. The episode exposes a basic ____: infrastructure built to be cheap and efficient was never designed to be defended.

In 1688 the Irish scientist William Molyneux, whose wife had lost her sight, sent the philosopher John Locke a question: suppose a man born blind has learned to distinguish a cube from a sphere by touch. If he were abruptly granted sight, could he tell which was which merely by looking, before touching them? Locke discussed the puzzle in his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, and he agreed with Molyneux that the answer was no. Knowledge of shape, both men thought, derives from experience, and a newly sighted person would not yet know how the look of an object corresponds to its feel. For three centuries the question remained a hypothetical exercise, debated by philosophers who had no means of testing it — until, in 2011, researchers working in India with children who had been born with treatable cataracts reported a direct test. Shortly after surgery gave them sight, the children could match shapes perfectly well by touch alone or by sight alone, but they matched a seen shape to a touched one only slightly better than chance. The connection between the two senses was at first <u>tenuous</u>. Within days, however, their performance improved markedly, suggesting that the brain learns to link touch and sight remarkably quickly once it has the chance.

In October 2024 the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the Peace Prize to Nihon Hidankyo, a Japanese organization of survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The survivors, known in Japanese as hibakusha, founded the group in 1956, more than a decade after the bombings, partly in response to radioactive fallout from American nuclear tests in the Pacific that had sickened Japanese fishermen. For nearly seventy years its members have traveled the world recounting their stories: of the flash and the heat, of relatives who vanished, of ailments that emerged years later, and of the discrimination many endured in marriage and work. The committee commended the group for helping to establish what is sometimes called the nuclear taboo, the potent norm that nuclear weapons must never be used again. It also noted, with some urgency, that this norm is under pressure, as several states modernize their arsenals and leaders issue overt threats. Time poses another difficulty: the average age of the surviving hibakusha is now well over eighty, and within a generation no one will be left who can say, I was there. Many fear that once their voices fall silent, the memory of nuclear war will become ____, a matter of textbooks and statistics rather than of human faces.

In 1969 the French writer Georges Perec published La Disparition, a novel of some three hundred pages in which the letter e, the most common letter in French, never appears. Such a text is termed a lipogram, and writing one at that length is fiendishly difficult: Perec had to <u>eschew</u> countless ordinary words, including the French words for he, she, and the. The plot itself is a sly joke about the constraint. It follows a group of characters searching for a missing friend, and members of the group begin to disappear whenever they come close to naming what is absent. Perec belonged to Oulipo, a circle of writers and mathematicians founded in Paris in 1960 who believed that stringent rules, far from stifling creativity, could provoke it. Yet many readers have discerned something more than a game in his novel. Perec's father was killed in the Second World War, and his mother was deported to Auschwitz when he was a small child; he grew up surrounded by an absence he could not name. Read in this light, a book organized around a vanished letter becomes a meditation on loss. The English writer Gilbert Adair later translated it, also without a single e, under the title A Void.

In 1954 a small group in the American Midwest became convinced, through messages its leader said she received from another planet, that a great flood would destroy much of the world before dawn on December 21. Its members believed that they alone would be evacuated by a flying saucer, and some quit their jobs and disposed of their possessions. The psychologist Leon Festinger and two colleagues, intrigued by how believers would respond when the prophecy failed, infiltrated the group without revealing their purpose and observed it. Midnight passed, and no saucer materialized. After hours of anguish, the leader announced a new message: the little group had spread so much light that God had spared the world. What happened next fascinated Festinger: members who had previously shunned publicity began phoning newspapers and seeking converts. Rather than abandoning their faith, many of the most devout clung to it more fervently. Festinger explained this with his theory of cognitive dissonance: when beliefs clash with clear evidence, the discomfort impels people to reduce the conflict, and those who have sacrificed the most often find it easier to <u>reinterpret the evidence than to admit the loss</u>. Later researchers have questioned the rigor of the study's methods, since the observers' presence may itself have influenced the group.

Conventional computers store information in bits that are either 0 or 1. Quantum computers use qubits, which can exist in combinations of both states at once and become linked to one another in ways that have no everyday equivalent. In principle this allows certain calculations, such as simulating molecules, to be performed far faster than any conventional machine could manage; in practice, however, qubits are maddeningly delicate. Heat, vibration, or stray electromagnetic signals can disrupt them within a tiny fraction of a second, introducing errors that proliferate as more qubits are added. For decades physicists have hoped to solve this with error correction, combining many physical qubits into a single, more reliable logical qubit. The catch is that every added qubit is another chance for error. In December 2024 Google reported that its new chip, Willow, had crossed a pivotal threshold: as the groups of qubits grew larger, the error rate went down rather than up. The company also said the chip had finished a benchmark calculation in under five minutes that would take a leading supercomputer an unimaginably long time. Independent experts lauded the error-correction result but noted that the benchmark had no practical use. Useful quantum computers, they cautioned, are still ____: promising, but far from ready for everyday work.

"Don't open the back until the film is rewound," the man at the camera shop said, sliding my grandfather's old camera across the counter. It had lain in a drawer for twenty years, and I had brought it in only because the shutter still clicked. He sold me a single roll of film, thirty-six frames, and wished me luck in a tone that implied I would need it. I was accustomed to a phone that let me take two hundred pictures of a sunset and delete one hundred and ninety-nine. Now every press of the button cost something, and there was no screen to tell me whether I had failed. It took me a month to finish the roll: my grandmother in her garden, the fish market at dawn, my sister asleep on a train. Each time I dithered so long that the moment almost passed. A community center nearby ran a darkroom class on Thursday evenings. Winding the film onto the developing reel in total darkness, I fumbled so badly and my nervousness was so <u>palpable</u> that the instructor, an elderly woman, began to hum quietly beside me. When the negatives finally hung up to dry, a third of them were blurred — but the portrait of my grandmother was sharp, and I have never deleted it, because there was never any way to.

In English a speaker can say It rained last night without revealing how she knows: perhaps she heard the rain, perhaps she saw the wet streets in the morning, or perhaps a neighbor told her. Many languages do not tolerate such vagueness; in grammatical systems known as evidentials, speakers must mark the source of their information. Turkish, for example, uses one past-tense ending for events the speaker witnessed and another for events learned from others or inferred from traces. Some Amazonian languages go much further, with separate endings for what was seen, heard, inferred, assumed, or reported. Linguists have long speculated whether such grammar shapes how speakers think. Some studies suggest that children learning evidential languages begin using the markers early but grasp the ideas behind them only later, around the age when they also understand that other people can hold false beliefs. Speakers of these languages sometimes say that English sounds oddly careless, since a sentence without an evidential seems to conceal whether the speaker is a witness or merely passing on gossip. English speakers can of course make the same distinctions when they wish, by adding words such as apparently or I saw. For speakers of evidential languages, however, the distinction is ____, built into the verb itself.

Common sense says that adding a road to a congested network should alleviate congestion, and removing one should make it worse. In 1968 the German mathematician Dietrich Braess showed that this is not always true: in certain networks, opening a new shortcut can make every driver's journey slower. The reason is that each driver, choosing the route that is quickest for himself, converges on the new link, and the resulting equilibrium can be worse for everyone than the one before. No driver has any incentive to change course, yet all would be better off if the shortcut did not exist — a finding now known as Braess's paradox. Real cities have furnished some striking illustrations. In Seoul, an elevated highway that carried large volumes of traffic over the Cheonggyecheon stream was demolished in 2003, and the buried stream was restored as a public park and walkway, opening in 2005. Critics had prophesied gridlock. Instead, traffic in the area did not worsen as feared, partly because drivers altered their routes, timing, or modes of travel, and partly because some trips simply disappeared. Engineers caution that the paradox holds only under particular conditions, and that removing roads is not a universal cure. But the episode helped persuade planners that road capacity and traffic speed are not linked as simply as once assumed.

A piano tuned today is, strictly speaking, slightly out of tune, and the reason lies in an awkward quirk of acoustics. Intervals that sound perfectly pure, such as the octave and the fifth, rest on simple ratios between frequencies, but stacking twelve pure fifths does not quite bring you back to the starting note seven octaves higher; a small gap is left over. Tuning systems are different ways of concealing that gap. For centuries many keyboard instruments were tuned so that the most common keys sounded beautifully pure, while remote keys sounded so harsh that composers simply shunned them. Equal temperament solves the problem by spreading the gap evenly across all twelve notes, so that every key sounds equally tolerable, if never perfectly pure. Johann Sebastian Bach's collection The Well-Tempered Clavier, with preludes and fugues in all twenty-four major and minor keys, is often cited as an early celebration of the latitude such tunings permitted, although historians contend that Bach in all likelihood used an unequal temperament in which each key kept a slightly different color. Some performers of early music prefer those older systems. To their ears equal temperament, for all its convenience, can sound a little <u>insipid</u>, as if every key had been painted the same shade of gray.

Consider two drivers who have each consumed several drinks at a party and drive home along similar roads with precisely the same degree of care, or negligence. One arrives home safely. The other, through no further fault of his own, meets a child who runs into the street, and the child is killed. Most people condemn the second driver far more harshly, and the law punishes him far more severely — yet the two committed precisely the same act; the only difference lay in contingencies neither of them controlled. The philosophers Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel called this problem moral luck, and it unsettles a widely held principle, that people should be judged only for what lies within their control; if we applied that principle rigorously, we would have to judge the two drivers equally. If we abandon it, we must admit that our moral standing hinges partly on luck. Neither alternative is palatable, and the tension, Nagel argued, cannot simply be argued away.

In June 2025 a new observatory on a mountaintop in Chile released its first images, unveiling luminous clouds of gas and millions of distant galaxies in exquisite detail. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory carries the largest digital camera ever built for astronomy, and its mission is unconventional. Rather than studying a few objects closely, it will sweep across the whole sky visible from the Southern Hemisphere again and again, returning to each patch every few nights for a decade, producing a kind of time-lapse film of the cosmos. Astronomers anticipate that it will detect vast numbers of asteroids, supernovae, and other objects that move or change. The observatory is named after the American astronomer Vera Rubin, whose measurements of how swiftly stars revolve within galaxies furnished some of the most compelling early evidence for dark matter, an invisible form of matter that appears to outweigh ordinary matter several times over. Fittingly, mapping the influence of dark matter is among the observatory's principal goals.

One of the earliest photographs to include a human being was taken almost by accident. In 1838 Louis Daguerre pointed his camera from a high window at the Boulevard du Temple, one of the busiest streets in Paris. The image depicts rows of buildings and trees, yet the street itself looks eerily deserted. The reason was the exposure time: the plate needed several minutes to record a scene, so carriages and pedestrians moving along the boulevard left no trace. Only one figure remained stationary long enough to be captured, a man near a corner who appears to be having his boots polished, together with the faint silhouette of the person polishing them. Neither could have known that he was being recorded. Today the picture is often heralded as the first photograph of a person, although historians concede that other early images may also have caught people and simply not survived.

How can we ascertain whether an animal recognizes itself? In 1970 the psychologist Gordon Gallup devised a deceptively simple test. After chimpanzees had grown used to a mirror, he anesthetized them and painted a red mark on a brow or ear that they could not see without a reflection. When they woke and looked into the mirror, they touched the mark on their own bodies, suggesting that they understood the image to be themselves. Monkeys subjected to the same test generally failed. Since then a handful of other species have passed, including some elephants, dolphins, and magpies, and in 2019 researchers controversially reported success with a small reef fish. Critics argue that the test is skewed toward animals that rely on vision. Dogs, which navigate the world chiefly through smell, usually disregard their reflections, yet they can discriminate their own scent from that of other dogs. Failing the mirror test, then, may reveal more about the test than about the animal.

For more than two centuries the one-cent coin was a fixture of American life, but in 2025 the United States resolved to stop minting it. In February the president directed the Treasury to end production, noting that each penny now cost nearly four cents to manufacture and distribute, and in November the Mint struck its final pennies for circulation. The decision capped years of debate. Economists had long pointed out that the coin has negligible purchasing power, that many people leave pennies in jars or simply refuse them as change, and that the government lost money on every one it produced. Defenders argued that abolishing the coin would compel shops to round cash prices upward, surreptitiously costing consumers money, although studies of countries that had already jettisoned their smallest coins, such as Canada in 2013, found little evidence of that. The billions of pennies already in circulation remain legal tender, though some businesses have begun rounding cash totals to the nearest five cents.

For most of the twentieth century, archaeologists assumed a clear chronology: people first learned to farm, then settled in villages, and only after that, with surplus food and organized labor, built monumental temples. Göbekli Tepe, a hilltop site in southeastern Turkey, overturned that sequence. Excavations led by the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt from the mid-1990s unearthed rings of massive T-shaped limestone pillars, some towering more than five meters and carved with foxes, boars, snakes, and vultures. The oldest structures date to around 9500 BCE, before pottery, metal tools, or the wheel, and apparently before farming had taken hold in the region. The builders seem to have been hunter-gatherers — and Schmidt conjectured that the need to provision large gatherings at the site may itself have encouraged the cultivation of wild cereals. Later research has found evidence of dwellings and cisterns nearby, suggesting that the site was not only a ceremonial center but also a place where people lived.

Look at a photograph of five friends at a party, and each face may seem more attractive than it would if you saw it alone. In 2014 two psychologists tested this impression, which had been named the cheerleader effect after a popular television sitcom. Volunteers evaluated the attractiveness of faces shown either in group photographs or cut out and displayed on their own. The same faces received higher ratings when they appeared in a group, and the researchers postulated an explanation grounded in how vision works: when we see several similar objects together, the brain tends to summarize them, computing a kind of average. Average faces, earlier studies had shown, are generally deemed attractive, because their irregularities cancel out. Seen in a crowd, each face is pulled slightly toward that pleasing average in our perception. In other words, <u>the group quietly lends each member its average</u>, smoothing over the idiosyncrasies that stand out when a face is viewed alone.

Hydrogen has been called the fuel of the future for so long that the phrase has become something of a joke. Burned or used in a fuel cell, it releases energy with water as its only direct by-product, and it can be stored and shipped in ways that electricity cannot. The difficulty lies in making it: almost all the hydrogen produced today is extracted from natural gas in a process that releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, while so-called green hydrogen, made by splitting water with electricity from renewable sources, avoids those emissions but remains considerably more expensive. Partly for this reason, enthusiasm has shifted. Hydrogen cars, once touted as rivals to battery vehicles, have largely lost that race, since using electricity directly in a battery wastes far less energy than converting it into hydrogen and back again. Many analysts now contend that hydrogen should be reserved for tasks that are hard to electrify, such as making fertilizer, refining fuel, and producing steel; in Sweden a pilot plant has already made steel with hydrogen instead of coal. Even in these areas, however, several large projects announced with great fanfare have been delayed or cancelled as costs escalated. The fuel of the future, it seems, will be ____ rather than universal: valuable in particular niches, but not the answer to every energy problem.

In July 1962 the French geologist Michel Siffre, then twenty-three, descended into an underground glacier in the Alps and remained there in solitude for about two months. He took no clock or watch. Whenever he woke, ate, or went to sleep, he telephoned a team on the surface, who recorded the times but were forbidden to divulge anything about them. The results astonished everyone, including Siffre. His body maintained a fairly regular rhythm of sleeping and waking, but each cycle ran somewhat longer than twenty-four hours, so that his internal days slowly drifted out of step with the sun. When the team finally told him that the experiment was over, he believed it was a date nearly a month earlier; he had lost track of roughly twenty-five days. His experience helped substantiate that humans possess an internal clock that keeps time on its own, though it needs daylight to remain accurately calibrated. Siffre was nothing if not <u>tenacious</u>. Despite the cold, the damp, and the isolation, which left him grappling with lapses of memory and bouts of melancholy, he returned to caves for subsequent experiments in later decades, including one in his sixties.

In April 1964, at the age of thirty-one, the Canadian pianist Glenn Gould gave a recital in Los Angeles and then never performed in public again. He was at the height of his fame. His 1955 recording of Bach's Goldberg Variations, played with startling clarity and velocity, had become one of the best-selling classical albums of its time, and concert halls around the world clamored for him. Gould, however, had come to detest the concert as an institution. He found the atmosphere competitive, even predatory, as if part of the audience were waiting for a mistake, and he believed that a live performance, heard once and then gone, was a poor way to present music. For the rest of his life he confined himself mainly to recording studios, where he could play a passage many times and splice together the best versions, much as a film director assembles scenes. Critics accused him of misleading listeners. Gould retorted that a recording was a different art form from a concert, as a film is from a play, and that the listener at home, free to replay and reflect, would become <u>a participant rather than a witness</u>. He also became known for humming audibly as he played, a habit his engineers never managed to expunge from the tapes; in 1981, a year before his death, he recorded the Goldberg Variations again, far more slowly.

Few questions polarize the artificial intelligence industry as sharply as whether powerful models should be released openly. When a company publishes a model's weights, the vast tables of numbers that govern its behavior, anyone with enough computing power can download, study, modify, and run it. Meta adopted this approach with its Llama models, and in early 2025 the Chinese firm DeepSeek startled the industry by releasing a formidable reasoning model whose weights were freely available. Advocates of openness advance several arguments. Independent researchers can scrutinize open models for flaws instead of trusting a company's assurances; small firms and universities can build on them without paying exorbitant fees; and power over a pivotal technology is not concentrated in a handful of corporations. Detractors reply that once weights are published they cannot be retracted, and the safety filters built into a model can be stripped away by anyone determined to use it for <u>nefarious</u> purposes, such as producing more convincing scams. Even the terminology is contested. In 2024 the Open Source Initiative, which has long defined what counts as open-source software, issued a definition for AI that requires enough information about training data to allow a model to be rebuilt, a standard that many so-called open models do not meet.

In 1842 Queen Victoria welcomed the German composer Felix Mendelssohn to Buckingham Palace and sang one of his songs for him — she chose Italien, which she said was her favorite — and Mendelssohn, mortified, confessed that the song was not his. It had been written by his elder sister, Fanny, and published under his name years earlier, along with several of her other songs. Fanny Mendelssohn was, by many accounts, as gifted as her brother; both received a rigorous musical education as children, but their paths soon diverged. Their father wrote to her that music might become Felix's profession, whereas for her it could only ever be an ornament, never the foundation of her life. The social expectations imposed on a woman of her class pointed the same way. Fanny nevertheless composed more than four hundred works, and she organized private Sunday concerts at the family home in Berlin where many of them were heard. Only in 1846, encouraged by friends, did she begin publishing music under her own name, but she died suddenly the following year, at forty-one. For more than a century her reputation remained ____, and much of her music has been performed and recorded only in recent decades.

In 1955 the British historian C. Northcote Parkinson published a satirical essay in The Economist that began with a sentence still quoted in offices around the world: work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion. An elderly lady with a whole day free, he observed, might squander hours writing and sending a single postcard, a task a busy person would dispatch in minutes. Behind the jest lay a serious contention about organizations. Officials, Parkinson argued, want to multiply subordinates rather than rivals, and they create work for one another, so that the size of a bureaucracy grows irrespective of how much there is to do. His favorite example was the British Royal Navy, whose administrative staff grew substantially between 1914 and 1928 even as the number of its major warships dwindled sharply. Parkinson added a further observation, sometimes called the law of triviality. A committee asked to approve a costly nuclear reactor, he suggested, might pass it in minutes, because few members grasped its intricacies, and then wrangle at length over the cost of a bicycle shed, a subject everyone felt competent to discuss. Though his essays were written as satire, managers and economists have found them uncomfortably ____, and his phrases have entered everyday speech.

Coffee reached England in the mid-seventeenth century, and the first English coffeehouse is generally said to have opened in Oxford around 1650. Within a few decades hundreds had proliferated across London. For the price of a cup, customers could linger for hours, read the newspapers and pamphlets kept on the tables, and argue with strangers about politics, science, and commerce. Because a visitor could acquire an education in current affairs for about a penny, the coffeehouses were nicknamed penny universities. Particular houses attracted particular crowds. Scientists congregated at some, writers at others, and merchants and ship captains at a house run by Edward Lloyd, where reliable shipping news drew people who wanted to insure vessels and cargoes; the insurance market Lloyd's of London evolved from those gatherings. Not everyone approved of such establishments. In 1675 King Charles II, suspecting that coffeehouses were breeding grounds for dissent against his government, issued a proclamation ordering them closed. The public outcry was so vehement that the order was withdrawn within days, before it had even taken effect. For historians, the coffeehouses show how new social spaces can <u>disseminate</u> information and opinion far beyond the reach of official channels.

In August 2024 the World Health Organization declared the spread of mpox a public health emergency of international concern, its highest level of alarm. It was the second such declaration in two years. In 2022 a different lineage of the virus had spread rapidly across dozens of countries, mainly through close sexual contact, before cases plummeted with vaccination and changes in behavior. The 2024 alarm was driven by a newer strain spreading in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and adjacent countries, where it was afflicting adults and children alike. A day earlier, the African Union's public health agency had declared its own continental emergency, the first in its history. The disease causes fever and painful skin lesions and can be lethal, especially for young children and people with weakened immune systems. Efficacious vaccines exist, but in 2024 most doses were held by affluent countries, while the places with the greatest need had very few. Health officials pointed out that the same disparity had been evident during the Covid-19 pandemic. Donations and new purchases belatedly began to arrive, yet they amounted to only a fraction of what was required. Many experts argued that the episode showed once again that, against infectious disease, global ____ is not charity but self-protection.

The rehearsal hall smelled of rosin and wet umbrellas. I had enrolled in the community orchestra in October and had been placed, to my dismay, at the back of the second violins beside a man named Mr. Petrov, who was eighty-three and a veteran of forty years in a professional orchestra. I was certain he could hear every wrong note I played — and he could. For the first month he said nothing; then, during a break, he leaned toward me and pointed at a passage I had been fumbling for weeks. "You are playing the notes," he said, "but you are not listening to the cellos." I was baffled. He told me to stop staring at the page during the next run-through, to watch the cellists' bows instead, and to come in only when I could feel their phrase arriving. It felt preposterous. But when the passage came, I heard for the first time that my part was not a line of its own but an answer to theirs. At the concert in December I still played wrong notes, perhaps more than in rehearsal. Afterward Mr. Petrov shook my hand and said only, "Better. Now you are <u>inside the music</u>." I have tried to stay there ever since.

Of all the philosophers of ancient Greece, few left behind more stories and fewer writings than Diogenes of Sinope. None of his works are extant; what we know comes largely from anecdotes compiled centuries later, many of which may be exaggerated. According to these accounts, Diogenes lived in Athens in a large ceramic storage jar, owned almost nothing, and subsisted by begging. On seeing a child drink water from cupped hands, he is said to have thrown away his only cup, ashamed to have been outdone in simplicity. Diogenes belonged to a school later called the Cynics, from the Greek word for dog, an epithet he seems to have embraced. His <u>austere</u> way of life was not merely a personal preference but a form of argument. He believed that most human customs, wealth, and social rank were contrived, and that a person who needed nothing could not be manipulated by anyone. He made his case through public spectacle: he was said to roam the marketplace in daylight carrying a lamp, claiming to be searching for an honest man. When Alexander the Great supposedly visited him and asked what he could do for him, Diogenes replied that the king could step aside, since he was blocking the sunlight.

In January 2025 the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists moved the hands of its Doomsday Clock to eighty-nine seconds to midnight, the closest they have ever been to the symbolic hour of global catastrophe. The clock was created in 1947 by scientists, many of whom had worked on the first atomic bombs and sought to alert the public to the dangers they had helped to unleash. It was first set at seven minutes to midnight, and in the decades since, a board of experts has moved it forward and back in response to geopolitical events. It reached its farthest point, seventeen minutes, in 1991, after the end of the Cold War and new agreements to cut nuclear arsenals. Today the board's deliberations extend beyond nuclear weapons — its announcements also weigh climate change, biological threats, and the misuse of new technologies such as artificial intelligence. In 2025 it cited escalating nuclear tensions among major powers and the absence of tangible progress on several of these risks. Supporters say the clock remains an evocative way to condense intricate dangers into a single image that anyone can grasp. Critics reply that it quantifies nothing precisely, that its settings reflect the subjective judgments of a small coterie, and that a clock which has hovered near midnight for years risks making alarm ____ rather than galvanizing action.

In 1993 the psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues published a study of violin students at a music academy in Berlin. The best students, those their teachers expected to become international soloists, had accumulated far more hours of solitary, focused practice by the age of twenty than students who were merely good. Ericsson argued that expert performance is cultivated largely through what he called deliberate practice: effortful work on particular deficiencies, guided by a teacher and by immediate feedback, as opposed to simply playing pieces one already enjoys. The idea was later popularized, in simplified form, as a rule that ten thousand hours of practice can make anyone an expert, a version Ericsson himself repudiated. Later research has muddied the picture. A large meta-analysis published in 2014 synthesized dozens of studies and found that the amount of practice explained a substantial share of differences in performance in games such as chess and in music, a smaller share in sports, and very little in academic education and many professions. Other factors, including the age at which training starts, working memory, and perhaps genetic differences, are also implicated, though few researchers doubt that practice is indispensable. The debate centers on how much variance it explains, and which kinds of practice most reliably <u>fortify</u> performance.

On the morning of June 30, 1908, witnesses in a remote part of Siberia saw a column of blue light streak across the sky, followed by a flash and a shock wave that knocked people off their feet dozens of kilometers away. Near the Tunguska River, some eighty million trees were leveled across an expanse of more than two thousand square kilometers. Because the region was so inaccessible, and because Russia was soon engulfed by war and revolution, no scientific expedition reached the site until 1927. Its leader, Leonid Kulik, anticipated finding a great crater and a buried meteorite, but he found neither; instead, the fallen trees radiated outward from a central zone where some trunks still stood upright, denuded of their branches. Most scientists now surmise that a rocky or icy body from space exploded in the air several kilometers above the ground, releasing its energy before it could strike the surface.

The word gentrification was coined in 1964 by the British sociologist Ruth Glass to characterize what she observed happening in parts of London: middle-class newcomers buying up dilapidated working-class houses, renovating them, and gradually transforming the character of whole districts. Six decades later, the term has migrated to cities around the world, and it has rarely been more contested. Critics point to escalating rents that displace long-time residents and the small shops that served them, replacing hardware stores and cheap cafés with boutiques that few locals can afford. Some economists, however, have found that low-income residents of gentrifying neighborhoods are not always more likely to move away than residents of poorer areas that remain unchanged, and that those who stay may profit from safer streets and better services. The debate is partly empirical and partly a matter of values: whether a neighborhood belongs chiefly to those who live there now or to anyone willing to pay to move in.

For most of the twentieth century, doctors presumed that stomach ulcers were caused mainly by stress, spicy food, and excess acid; treatment consisted of bland diets, antacids, and in grave cases surgery, and ulcers often came back. Around 1982 the Australian pathologist Robin Warren and a young physician, Barry Marshall, proposed an alternative explanation: a spiral-shaped bacterium, later named Helicobacter pylori, that colonized the stomach lining of many ulcer patients. The idea met fierce resistance, since most experts were convinced that no bacterium could survive for long in such an acidic environment. Unable to infect laboratory animals, Marshall took a drastic step in 1984: he drank a culture of the bacteria, developed acute stomach inflammation within days, and then cured himself with antibiotics. Over the following decade the evidence accumulated and antibiotic treatment became standard; in 2005 the two men were awarded a Nobel Prize for their discovery.

For more than a century the diamond industry extolled its gems as rare, eternal, and the quintessential symbol of lasting love — a message that now faces an unprecedented challenge. Diamonds grown in laboratories, either by replicating the crushing pressure and heat deep inside the Earth or by depositing carbon atoms layer by layer from a gas, are chemically and physically identical to mined stones. Even trained jewelers cannot differentiate them without specialized equipment that detects subtle discrepancies in how the crystals grew. As production has burgeoned, the price of laboratory diamonds has fallen steeply, and in some markets they now constitute a large share of engagement rings. Mined diamonds have also become cheaper. Producers of natural stones argue that their gems carry a story billions of years in the making, while critics reply that much of the value of any diamond was always a matter of marketing rather than of scarcity.

When the Portuguese poet Fernando Pessoa died in Lisbon in 1935, he was known only to a small circle of readers, and just one book of his poetry in Portuguese had appeared under his own name. He left behind a trunk holding more than twenty-five thousand pages of manuscripts and typescripts, many of them written not as Pessoa at all. Over his lifetime he conceived dozens of literary personas, which he called heteronyms, each with its own biography, philosophy, and style. Alberto Caeiro was a country poet who distrusted thought and wished only to see things as they are; Ricardo Reis was a doctor who wrote restrained odes in a classical manner; Alvaro de Campos was a naval engineer whose poems teemed with noise and modern machines. These were not mere pseudonyms: Pessoa had them disagree with one another, critique one another's work, and he even cast their horoscopes. Scholars are still cataloguing the trunk's contents, and new texts continue to appear.

Why is water, without which no one can live, so cheap, while diamonds, which serve almost no utilitarian purpose, are so expensive? Adam Smith posed this conundrum in The Wealth of Nations in 1776, distinguishing between the value of a thing in use and its value in exchange. He did not fully resolve it. The resolution emerged about a century later, when several economists working independently, among them the Austrian Carl Menger and Léon Walras, a French economist working in Lausanne, developed the idea of marginal utility. What determines price, they argued, is not the total usefulness of a good but the usefulness of one more unit of it. Because water is usually abundant, an extra glass adds little to our well-being, so we will pay little for it; diamonds are scarce, so an additional one is prized. The calculus changes with circumstances: a traveler lost in a desert might gladly barter a diamond for a single bottle of water.

March 3. Experiment 14 failed, like the previous thirteen: the protein refuses to crystallize; every tray shows the same gray sludge, and my supervisor says nothing, which is worse than criticism; I have started to wonder whether I am simply not suited to this work.
March 9. Changed the temperature again. Nothing. A first-year student asked me how long it usually takes to get crystals, and I laughed in a way that frightened us both.
March 17. Tray 6, well C4: something glittering under the microscope. Too small to be sure. I did not tell anyone in case it vanishes by morning.
March 18. It did not disappear. Three tiny needles, sharp-edged and translucent. I photographed them eleven times. My supervisor scrutinized them for a long while and said, "Well. Now we have something to argue about." From him, that is practically an oration. I walked home in the rain without an umbrella and did not notice until I reached the door.

Weapons that can select and attack targets without a human decision at the moment of attack are no longer the stuff of science fiction. Rudimentary versions, such as defensive systems that automatically fire at incoming missiles, have existed for decades. What has changed is the proliferation of cheap drones and image-recognition software, which together make it possible to build machines that search for, identify, and strike targets autonomously. Reports from recent conflicts suggest that drones with increasing degrees of autonomy are already being deployed on the battlefield. Diplomats have deliberated over the issue since 2014 under a United Nations weapons convention in Geneva, but those talks operate by consensus, and a few states have been able to block binding rules. In December 2023 the UN General Assembly adopted its first resolution on lethal autonomous weapons, voicing apprehension about their risks, and the UN Secretary-General and the International Committee of the Red Cross jointly urged states to conclude a treaty by 2026. Many proposals revolve around the idea of meaningful human control: a person, not an algorithm, should remain responsible for decisions to use lethal force. Opponents of a ban contend that well-designed systems might make fewer errors than fatigued or frightened soldiers. Supporters reply that the real danger lies in removing ____ from killing, so that no identifiable person answers for a machine's mistake.

In 2014 a British company unveiled Vantablack, a coating made of tiny carbon tubes standing upright like a dense forest. Light entering the forest ricochets between the tubes until almost all of it is absorbed, and the original coating reflected only a minute fraction of the light that struck it. Objects covered in it seem to lose their shape and become flat holes in space. The substance itself was engineered for a scientific purpose: suppressing stray light in telescopes and satellite instruments. The art world took a different interest. In 2016 the sculptor Anish Kapoor acquired the exclusive right to use a version of Vantablack in art, and many artists were incensed that a single person could monopolize a color. One of them, the painter Stuart Semple, responded by releasing a vivid pink pigment that anyone could buy, except, according to its terms of sale, Anish Kapoor. Semple went on to produce affordable ultra-black paints of his own for general sale. The dispute raised a weighty question in a whimsical form. Artists have always depended on the materials at their disposal, but when a pigment is a patented industrial product rather than a pulverized mineral, access to color can become a matter of legal ____ rather than of skill.

In June 2024 two veteran NASA astronauts, Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, launched to the International Space Station aboard Boeing's Starliner capsule on its first crewed test flight. The visit was supposed to last about a week; during the approach to the station, however, several of the capsule's thrusters failed and small helium leaks were detected. Engineers spent weeks analyzing the malfunctions, and ultimately NASA concluded that bringing the crew home in Starliner was too risky. The capsule returned to Earth uncrewed in September, touching down safely, while the two astronauts remained on the station, where their stay was prolonged to more than nine months. They finally came home in March 2025 aboard a SpaceX Dragon capsule. Much of the public coverage described them as stranded, a word both astronauts politely rejected. They were seasoned professionals, they pointed out, aboard a well-supplied station, and they spent the extra months on routine station work, from experiments to repairs and spacewalks. The episode nevertheless dealt a blow to Boeing, whose program had already endured years of delays and cost overruns, and it underscored NASA's reliance on a single company for crew transport. Space agencies have long argued that keeping two independent ways to reach orbit is a matter of ____, not luxury.

In the early 1960s geologists began reporting an anomaly. Rocks deposited by glaciers, with their characteristic jumble of striated stones, kept turning up in layers roughly seven hundred million years old in places that, according to magnetic evidence, had then lain close to the equator. If ice had reached the tropics, had the whole planet frozen over? For years many geologists considered the idea barely <u>tenable</u>. A frozen Earth would reflect so much sunlight back into space that it should have stayed frozen forever, yet life evidently survived and the ice eventually vanished. In 1992 the geologist Joseph Kirschvink gave the hypothesis its memorable name, Snowball Earth, and proposed a way out: even on an icy planet, volcanoes would continue to emit carbon dioxide. With oceans sealed under ice and little exposed rock to absorb the gas, it would slowly accumulate over millions of years until the greenhouse effect became potent enough to melt the ice, perhaps quite abruptly. Anomalous layers of carbonate rock lying directly on top of the glacial deposits seem to chronicle that abrupt warming, though debate continues over whether the oceans froze completely or left open water near the equator, a version some call Slushball Earth.

Deep in the Brazilian Amazon, a few hundred people speak Pirahã, a language unrelated to any other living tongue. Much of what the outside world knows about it comes from Daniel Everett, an American who arrived in the 1970s as a missionary, spent years immersed among the Pirahã, and eventually became a linguist and renounced his religious faith. In 2005 Everett published a paper that provoked one of the fiercest debates in modern linguistics. He reported that Pirahã appeared to lack recursion, the ability to place one phrase or clause inside another of the same kind, as in the sentence I think that you said that it rained. Many linguists, following Noam Chomsky, had treated recursion as the defining feature shared by all human languages. Everett also claimed that the language had no words for exact numbers, only terms meaning roughly a small amount and a larger amount, and he attributed these features to a culture focused on immediate experience. Critics retorted sharply. Some reanalyzed his own recordings and argued that Pirahã does contain embedded structures, while others noted that few outsiders could verify his claims because so few people speak the language. The dispute remains unresolved, partly because the evidence comes from so ____ a source.

For sale: baby shoes, never worn. These six words are often called the shortest story ever written, and they are almost always attributed to Ernest Hemingway. According to a popular legend, he wrote them to win a bet with fellow writers who doubted that a complete story could be told in so few words. The tale is beguiling, and it fits Hemingway's reputation for <u>terse</u> prose, stripped of ornament and full of meaning left unsaid. Unfortunately, there is no evidence that he ever wrote it. The anecdote about the bet did not appear in print until decades after his death, and researchers have unearthed newspaper notices with strikingly similar wording from the early twentieth century, when Hemingway was still a child. The real history is in some ways more intriguing. Small advertisements were charged by the word, so sellers had every reason to be concise, and a notice offering unused baby clothes could allude to a private grief that the advertiser never spelled out. Readers seem to have felt the poignant power of such lines long before anyone credited them to a famous author. Today the phrase has spawned whole collections of six-word memoirs, in which ordinary people try to sum up their lives in the same compressed form.

Venezuela once had six glaciers high in the Andes, in the Sierra Nevada de Mérida — but by the twenty-first century only one remained, the Humboldt glacier, and it was receding fast. In 2024 scientists reported that it had dwindled to less than two hectares, far too small to be classified as a glacier, and it was reclassified as an ice field. With that, Venezuela became the first country in modern times known to have lost all of its glaciers. Researchers anticipate that others will follow; small glaciers in countries such as Indonesia, Mexico, and Slovenia are also shrinking. In late 2023 the Venezuelan government had attempted a salvage operation, covering part of the remaining ice with a large thermal blanket meant to reflect sunlight and slow the melting. Scientists were skeptical. The ice was already too diminished to salvage, they said, and the blanket might shed plastic fibers into the fragile mountain environment. Above all, they argued, such measures address <u>the symptom rather than the disease</u>: tropical glaciers are vanishing because the planet is warming, and no covering on a single mountainside can change that. The loss is partly symbolic, since the glacier furnished little water, but it also eliminates a habitat and a landmark cherished by local communities for generations.

It is often said that William Shakespeare invented thousands of English words, and the claim has a reputable source. When the editors of the great Oxford English Dictionary began compiling examples in the nineteenth century, they relied heavily on eminent authors, and Shakespeare's works had been studied more closely than almost any other texts of his time. As a result, his plays often furnished the earliest recorded example of a word, and readers understandably inferred that he had coined it. The digital age has muddied this picture. Once millions of pages of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century books, pamphlets, and sermons were scanned and made searchable, researchers found many supposedly Shakespearean words in texts written years or decades before his plays. Such discoveries <u>belie</u> the popular image of a lone genius stocking the language single-handedly. Shakespeare was still an extraordinary innovator. He combined existing words in fresh ways, turned nouns into verbs with remarkable audacity, and gave phrases a memorable form that ensured their survival. But he worked within a language that was expanding rapidly on its own, as writers borrowed freely from Latin, French, and other tongues. His real achievement, many scholars now maintain, was less to invent new words than to show what could be done with them.

Few countries have embraced digital payment as enthusiastically as Sweden. Cash now accounts for only a meager share of purchases there, many shops and cafés refuse banknotes altogether, and a mobile payment app is used by most of the adult population. For a time, Sweden was held up as a paragon of the cashless future, and its efficiency is undeniable: digital transactions are fast, easy to record, and difficult for criminals to hide. Lately, however, Swedish authorities have begun to have second thoughts, partly because some groups find digital payment daunting, including many elderly people, recent immigrants without bank accounts, and people with certain disabilities. A more pressing worry, though, concerns resilience. If power grids or communication networks falter, through storms, technical faults, or a deliberate attack, a society that has abandoned cash may find itself unable to procure food or medicine. Sweden's central bank has urged lawmakers to make sure that essential services continue to accept cash, and civil defense guidance encourages households to keep a small amount at home for emergencies. These efforts do not reflect antipathy toward technology. Their aim, which most observers consider <u>laudable</u>, is to ensure that convenience for the many does not become a snare for the vulnerable or a weakness in a crisis.

In the summer of 1954 the social psychologist Muzafer Sherif conducted an experiment at a camp in Robbers Cave State Park in Oklahoma. Twenty-two eleven-year-old boys, homogeneous in background and strangers to one another, were divided into two groups and brought to the camp separately. For about a week each group bonded on its own, choosing a name, the Eagles and the Rattlers, and developing its own customs. Then the researchers introduced a tournament of competitive games with prizes for the winners, and hostility escalated quickly: the groups burned each other's flags, ransacked each other's cabins, and refused to eat together. Simply bringing the boys together for pleasant activities, such as watching films, did not defuse the conflict. What worked, Sherif reported, were superordinate goals, problems that neither group could solve alone, such as repairing a broken water supply or pooling money to rent a film. Cooperation on such tasks gradually eroded the rivalry. Later scholars have pointed out that Sherif's earlier attempt at a similar study had collapsed when the boys turned against the staff instead, and that the experimenters orchestrated events more than their reports acknowledged. The study remains influential, but perhaps more as a vivid illustration than as ____ proof.

Ludwig van Beethoven began to lose his hearing in his late twenties, and by his late forties he could barely follow a conversation. From about 1818 his visitors therefore wrote their side of the exchange in notebooks, while Beethoven usually answered aloud. Some four hundred of these conversation books are thought to have existed, and the roughly 140 that survive are an invaluable record. They capture discussions of politics, money, his nephew's tribulations, and his music, along with shopping lists and grievances about servants — yet they are also a cautionary tale about historical sources. After Beethoven's death, his secretary and early biographer Anton Schindler retained the books, and he destroyed many of them. Worse, in the 1970s scholars ascertained that Schindler had added entries of his own after the composer's death, fabricating conversations that made himself appear a closer and more trusted friend than he had been. Some of the best-known anecdotes about Beethoven turned out to rest on these forgeries; yet the surviving genuine pages also enrich our sense of the man. At the premiere of his Ninth Symphony in 1824, Beethoven, unable to hear the applause, had to be turned around to see the audience on its feet, a scene that the books help to place within the long silence of his later years.

Does health insurance make people healthier? The question sounds straightforward, but it is hard to answer, because people who have insurance differ from those who do not in income, education, and myriad other ways. In 2008 the state of Oregon inadvertently created an ideal test. Having funds to enroll only some of the low-income adults who wanted to join its public insurance program, it held a lottery, randomly drawing names from a waiting list of about ninety thousand people. Researchers then compared the winners, who could apply for coverage, with those who were not chosen; the results, published over the following years, were mixed. Within two years, those given access to insurance used more health care, including doctor visits and prescriptions; they were far less likely to face catastrophic medical bills, and rates of depression were appreciably lower. However, the study found no statistically significant improvement in measures such as blood pressure and cholesterol. Each side of the American health care debate seized on the findings that bolstered its position. Many economists argued that the most <u>germane</u> result was the reduction in financial strain, since protecting people from ruinous costs is the fundamental purpose of insurance.
